parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you tell me which company you work for, and walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you from start to finish?

I work at one of the drone operating companies. Regulators can ask my company to show how our drones have been looked after, and my work includes keeping drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge.
How does your day usually start, and how do you know which drones or charging pads need your attention first?
I don't know.
How do you find out that a drone needs to be taken out of service for repairs, or that it needs to be sent to charge?
I don't know.
Who hands work to you during the day, and who do you hand work off to?
I don't know.
Could you walk me through what you actually do when you add a new drone to the fleet or set up a charging pad at a site?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and I handle adding new drones to the fleet and setting up charging pads at our sites. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians like me, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after. I also retire old ones, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge.
When regulators ask your company to show how your drones have been looked after, what specific information or records do you have to show them?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
What happens when a drone is out of service for repairs—how do other people in your company know it can't be used?
I don't know.
What do you currently check by hand in your daily work because you don't trust a system or someone else's word?
I don't know.
What are you most afraid a new service or software tool might get wrong in your work?
I don't know.
Right after something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what is the very first thing you need to know?
I don't know.
Is there anything else you can tell me about the drones, the charging pads, the sites, or the work you do?

I run a fleet of a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers that differ in carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors, and charging connectors. We have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites, and our drones have a home site. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
Could you tell me more about the charging pads and how they match up with the different drone models and connectors?

Our drones use several connector types that are not interchangeable because they differ from model to model. We have our own charging pads at our own sites, a few dozen of them in total. Pads are never lent to another company.
When you send a drone to charge, how do you decide which charging pad to send it to, and what happens if a pad is already in use or out of order?
I don't know.
Could you tell me more about the sites and what it means for a drone to have a home site?
Each of our drones has a home site, and we have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites. Pads are never lent to another company.
Can a drone charge or be serviced at any of your company's sites, or only at its home site?
I don't know.
What else can you tell me about how you manage repairs, servicing, or retiring drones?

I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and I retire old ones. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians like me. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
What else can you tell me about the charging pads and keeping them in working order?

I keep charging equipment in working order alongside the drones, and I set up charging pads at our company's sites. Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, numbering a few dozen. Pads are never lent to another company.
Are there any other details about your role, your company, or the fleet that you haven't mentioned yet?

I work at one of the drone operating companies where I keep drones and charging equipment in working order. My role includes adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge.
